body.text: The steps to take as interest rates rise and mortgages become unaffordable
Every contestant in the TV series Alone steps straight off the boat — in a remote location where they must survive 'alone' with only 10 items — and immediately prioritises building shelter.

Not fishing, not foraging for food, not even lighting a fire, but assembling some tree branches to sling a good ol' tarp (invariably one of the 10 chosen items) across to protect themselves from the elements.
Their reasoning is sound: get wet, get cold, and you are a goner. As threats to your mortality go, hypothermia beats hunger or dehydration every day.
Housing is the most fundamental of our human needs, making it perhaps the highest perversion of our policy settings in Australia that we have let home values climb so high relative to incomes.

Outside of a survivalist setting, housing provides a home where you feel safe to rest your head at night and where you feel warm, secure and protected. Home is also a place to care for your children, feel part of your community and help you reset after a day of work or caring responsibilities.
People who do not know where they are going to sleep at night cannot apply for jobs, make plans, feel part of the community or be fully mentally present for their children.
But you do not have to be jobless or homeless to feel the pinch of housing insecurity.
The housing game has changed
Even for those who have been lucky enough to make it onto the home ownership ladder, the average size of mortgages these days usually means a degree of financial stress.

Recent home buyers must contend with interest rates higher than anyone expected. Indeed, if you bought with a home loan on an interest rate of around 2 per cent, you have already smashed through the 3 percentage point 'stress test' banks typically apply when assessing affordability of new loans.
Historically, borrowers could rely on wage increases to do some of the heavy lifting in helping to put them ahead of their minimum repayments. But real wages have barely budged for the past decade.

Meanwhile, many of the first home buyers who rushed to take advantage of the government's 5 per cent deposit scheme are now sitting in 'negative equity' territory, where their home loan is bigger than the value of their home, which continues to fall.

The old financial wisdom of leveraging to the eyeballs to get a foot on the ladder to enjoy supersized home price rises has been fundamentally altered by the recent move to abolish negative gearing on purchases of established properties, which has seen investors exit the market in droves.
The hidden face of mortgage pain
Analysts assessing the pain being felt by households like to refer to arrears rates — the proportion of loans on which payments are overdue — of 'only' about 1 per cent or so.

But that is just the tip of the iceberg. Add in the borrowers in hardship arrangements, those running down their savings buffers, having to go without food, electricity or lifestyle expenses to prioritise paying the mortgage, and you find a real world of mortgage pain.
You may not be behind on the mortgage, but that does not mean you are not stressed.
Knowing your options when it comes to managing your mortgage can be a great stress reliever, even if you never need to use them.
Selling your home is not the only option

Many people who worry about their mortgages immediately jump to the conclusion they may have to sell their home, and for some, that may, ultimately, be their best option. But there are a world of options to consider first.

Of course, the most obvious way to try to keep ahead of repayments is to look for ways to either boost your income or cut your costs. Many Australians are juggling multiple jobs, picking up extra jobs in the 'gig' economy. For others, it means both parents working and juggling care and work responsibilities.
Make sure you are getting all the government rebates and payments you are entitled to by searching 'cost of living' and the name of your state or territory government.
Commit to tracking your spending to identify areas where you may be able to cut back. Shop around on the 'big rocks' on your budget for a better deal on electricity, insurance, phone and internet.
Consider selling other assets, like second cars, or renting out spare rooms.
Reach out to your lender
If you think you may miss a payment, reach out to your bank to discuss your options, such as extending the term of your loan or going interest-only for a period.
Banks sell mortgages on the assumption that life is linear — you have a certain income today, and that will remain the same for the entire 30 years of the life of the loan.
Rarely does that happen. Divorces, children, redundancies and ill health can all throw a spanner in the works.

While banks like to think they sell off-the-shelf 'financial products' these days, your mortgage is an ongoing financial service. Your bank needs to deal with you for richer or poorer, in sickness and health, as long as your mortgage shall live.
Lenders have not just an ethical duty, but a legal obligation to help you in times of hardship.
Know your financial hardship rights
If you contact your bank unable to make your repayments, they are legally required to consider you for 'financial hardship' and offer you reprieve.

Many people are worried that a financial hardship arrangement will affect their credit score. It will indeed be noted on your credit file, but it does not affect the calculation of your overall credit score and disappears once you cease your arrangement and get back to required repayments.
Failing to arrange an altered repayment plan and defaulting on your payments, by contrast, does negatively affect your credit score.

Banks have many options at their disposal to help you get through a rough patch, including lowering your interest rate, extending the length of your loan so your repayments are lower, converting to 'interest only' payments for a period of time and arranging a complete payment freeze and deferring interest payments (be aware that such changes can extend the life of your loan and mean higher interest over time).
In a perfect world, banks can also help you to consolidate debts and waive fees.
In the real world, a recent review by the corporate watchdog found the hardship processes of banks cumbersome, and many people drop out of the process.
In which case, knowing when to ask for help may just be your very best option.
Call a free financial counsellor

If you are struggling to pay your expenses and debts, you can call the National Debt Helpline on 1800 007 007 and connect to a free, confidential and independent financial counsellor. Financial counsellors are funded by charities, not-for-profit organisations and via government funding.
They can help speak to your lender on your behalf and lodge a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority if you are unhappy with their response to your request for hardship.
They can help to make sure your debts are legally owed, ie that you haven't been a victim of irresponsible lending or coerced into obtaining your debt.

They can help you put together a statement of your financial position to help you figure out your capacity to continue paying your loan. They can also point you in the right direction to access grants, emergency relief, free legal assistance and specialist services for help with gambling addiction, mental health, alcohol and other drugs support.
You are not alone
Sometimes selling your home may end up as the best option to get out of a mortgage you truly cannot afford. But a financial counsellor can help you to think through your options.

Amid the rising cost of living, an increasing proportion — more than a third — of calls to the National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) are coming from people who have paid work but are still worried about making ends meet.
In times like these, reaching out for help does not mean you are a failure or that you are not good with money. It might just be the most financially sound decision you ever make.
When it comes to managing your debts in a cost of living crisis, you do not have to go it alone.

The information presented in this article is of a general educational nature only and does not take into account your personal circumstances or present every option that might be available to you. Always seek appropriate advice specific to your situation before making any significant financial decisions.
